E0252.summary: A cited figure whose ladder Atwood uses as an image of ascending knowledge and identifies with the magnetic chain.
E0252.body: Atwood invokes “Celsus’ ladder” as an image of ascending knowledge [I.1 ¶64]. Later she identifies the magnetic chain with “that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven” [III.2 ¶54]. The book gives nothing else about Celsus.

E0253.summary: In the Table Talk, the center of substantial life which every creature seeks, which each person can find in himself at moments.
E0253.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of “the center of the substantial life which every creature is seeking” [APP ¶113]. She holds that “Every one can find in himself at moments the true center” [APP ¶115], apparently through deep thought, and that the same revelation is given to all who enter it [APP ¶115].

E0254.summary: Atwood's paired terms for the universal centre, from which the sensible world is an outbirth, and the circumference, where being's equilibrium is broken for manifestation.
E0254.body: Atwood sets the universal centre, from which the sensible world is an outbirth, against the circumference, where “the equilibrium of being is broken everywhere at the circumference for manifestation” [II.4 ¶50]. In the illumination she describes, the light spreads outward, “diffusing itself from the freed center outwardly center outwardly until it moved the dark circumference of sense itself” [II.4 ¶54]. The context suggests the work frees the centre so that its light reaches and moves the outer, sensible life. See also centers and circumferences; circulation.

E0255.summary: Paired terms Atwood uses in warning that the centers must not be stirred before the circumferences can conceive them.
E0255.body: Atwood warns against acting “lest the centers should be stirred up before the circumferences are ready to conceive them” [IV.1 ¶13]. The text does not explain the pair further here; compare center / circumference.

E0256.summary: That with which the Aqua Philosophica, once conjoined in consciousness, becomes all-powerful.
E0256.body: In a footnote Atwood says of the Aqua Philosophica that “being conjoined in consciousness with the central Efficient, it becomes all-powerful” [I.3 n36]. The term is not further defined.

E0257.summary: A fire within the will or nature: in the Table Talk, Lucifer's stirring of it burned up the ether; in Vaughan, it stands opposed to the moist natures.
E0257.body: Two voices use the term. Quoting Vaughan, the text says that when heat is excessive the moist natures “will stand up against the central fire, and the central fire against them” [III.4 ¶44], producing a division in the Chaos. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of Lucifer's fall as “the stirring up of the central fire in his will” [APP ¶133], which inflamed the vehicle of his life and burned up the ether. Both passages apparently treat the central fire as dangerous when wrongly roused.

E0258.summary: The inner force of the Universal Spirit, which repeated operations draw wholly out until it acts forcibly at the circumference.
E0258.body: Atwood describes repeated operations upon the Universal Spirit continued “until the central force, wholly drawn out, acts forcibly at the circumference” [IV.3 ¶29]. Compare center / circumference.

E0259.summary: That whose whole voluntary force alone can arrest the imaginative flux of freed vitality and compel it to repose.
E0259.body: Atwood says that to arrest the imaginative flux of the freed vitality “it need the whole voluntary force of the central magnet” [III.2 ¶24], and that “this alone, which is its proper reason, can compel it to repose” [III.2 ¶24]. The central magnet is thus apparently equated with “its proper reason”, though the referent of “its” is unclear from the passage.

E0260.summary: In the Moorish philosopher's words, something man may draw to himself in abundance; not further defined.
E0260.body: Quoting the Moorish philosopher, the text speaks of one “who is able to draw to himself the Central Salt of nature in abundance” [II.1 ¶9]. The term is not explained.

E0261.summary: The goal towards which consciousness is translated, beneath the sensible medium, by obscuration.
E0261.body: Atwood speaks of the need “to translate the consciousness underneath this medium by obscuration, towards the Central Source” [II.3 ¶5]. The context suggests the Central Source is the inward origin reached by withdrawing consciousness beneath the sensible medium.

E0262.summary: The voice of the Chaldaic oracles, which Atwood cites repeatedly in support of her account of the fire, the guide and light, and the threefold Art of Reason.
E0262.body:
Atwood cites the Chaldaic oracle often, always in support:

- That there are pure demons and that the products of evil matter are useful: “Natura suadet esse demonas puros, et malae materiae germina utilia et bona” [II.3 ¶24] (our translation: nature persuades that there are pure demons, and that the germs of evil matter are useful and good).
- That the practitioner should not heed apparitions: “he apply not his mind to it, nor esteem the voice proceeding thence to be true” [II.3 ¶20].
- On the guide and the promised light: “the mortal, approaching the fire, will have a light from divinity” [II.3 n37].
- In what she calls ‘operative language’, on fire, the intellectual pattern and the Presters of Intellectual Fire: “O how the world hath Intellectual guides inflexible!” [II.4 ¶31].
- As pursuing the same Art of Reason she describes (Monad, Duad, Triad, the Matrix and the Prester of Fire): “For the mind of the Father said that all things be cut into Three” [IV.2 ¶21].

See also Chaldaic Oracles.

E0263.summary: A collection of oracles Atwood cites for Latin verse on the life-bearing fire and, in the Table Talk, for the soul as the place where the law of Light is manifested.
E0263.body: Atwood cites the Oracula Chaldeor for Latin verse on “Vitifer Ignis” and a Centre [IV.1 ¶35]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she uses the Chaldaic Oracles in support of the soul as the place where the law of Light is manifested: “There is room for the image also in the circumlucid place. Every way to the unfashioned soul stretch the reins of fire” [APP ¶96]. Elsewhere in the Table Talk they are only referred to for comparison on the solution (‘Article Hecate, etc.’) [APP ¶50]. See also the Chaldaic oracle.

E0264.summary: A quoted term glossed as ‘steel’: the means of extracting ‘our sea water’ and, in Cosmopolite, the partner that conceives with gold.
E0264.body: Quoted voices only. In the passage citing Synesius and the New Light, the text speaks of “our chalybs, or steel” [I.2 ¶33], the means by which ‘our sea water’ is extracted; it is otherwise unexplained. In Cosmopolite (quoted via Eudoxus), after gold couples with ‘it’, “the Chalybes conceives and begets a son more glorious than the Father” [IV.3 ¶10]. The text does not say what the chalybs plainly is, beyond the gloss ‘steel’.

E0265.summary: In Eirenaeus, the product of the Dragon–Lodestone conjunction and purgations: ‘our Chaos’, containing all the Arcana in virtue, not yet in act.
E0265.body: Quoting the same author (Eirenaeus), the text says that after the conjunction of the Dragon and the Lodestone and the purgations, “Hence comes the Chamelion which is our Chaos, in which all the Arcana are contained; not in act as yet, but in virtue” [IV.1 ¶43]. So the Chamelion is identified with Chaos [IV.1 ¶43].

E0266.summary: The primeval thing, named by several voices; in Atwood it holds the two Principles, which may be dissevered if the internal agent wakes too soon and are to be united to a new Life.
E0266.body:
Several voices use the term:

- Khunrath (quoted): when the process is done rightly, “the new Chaos of the Universal Nature” appears unfolded and separated [III.3 ¶9].
- Ovid (quoted): “Me Chaos antiqui, nam res sum prisca, vocabant.” [III.3 ¶45] (our translation: the ancients called me Chaos, for I am a thing of old). In the same paragraph the metropolitan of Memphis gives an account in which the ‘primeval parent’, moved by the breath of Erebus, brought forth Hyle and Eros.
- Vaughan (quoted): when moist natures and central fire are set against each other, “there will be a terrible division in the Chaos” [III.4 ¶44].
- Atwood: if the internal agent wakes too soon there may be “a disseveration in the Chaos, and the two Principles stand up one against the other” [IV.1 ¶15].
- Uncertain voice: “Learn to unite the Principles of our Chaos to a new Life” [IV.2 ¶18], to be regenerated by Water and the Spirit.

The records differ: Khunrath speaks of the Chaos appearing unfolded and separated in the right process, while Vaughan and Atwood warn of a premature division of its Principles. Eirenaeus identifies the Chamelion with ‘our Chaos’ [IV.1 ¶43].

E0267.summary: In Vaughan, the nurse of Faith: charitable works yield hope of heaven, and hope leads to belief.
E0267.body: Quoting Vaughan, the text says “as God is the Father, so Charity is the nurse of Faith” [III.4 ¶44]: charitable works yield hope of heaven, and hope leads to belief.

E0268.summary: Mentioned in the Table Talk as being Jupiter and Lune, and as one who ought to have reworked her sister's book.
E0268.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Charlotte Bronte is said to be Jupiter and Lune and to have ought to rework her sister's book [APP ¶175].

E0269.summary: Author of the Breviary of Philosophy, whom Atwood cites on the nested vessels, instructing the potter, and the value of a faithful servant.
E0269.body: Atwood cites Charnocke’s Breviary of Philosophy in illustration. From chap. 1, on the nested vessels and the need to instruct the potter: “One within another, it is a pretty feate, The Third without them to guide up the heate” [III.4 ¶33]. From chap. 3 (‘Idem’), on the trouble with indifferent assistants and the worth of a faithful servant [III.4 ¶34–35].

E0270.summary: Cited for the tale of the Chanon’s Yeoman, which Atwood uses to illustrate the boastings and beliefs of ignorance.
E0270.body: Atwood cites Chaucer’s tale of the Chanon’s Yeoman as illustrating the boastings and beliefs of ignorance about the art [I.1 ¶64].

E0271.summary: Unattributed Latin verse on Cheiron, teacher of Achilles, whom Atwood reads as Power and Motive in alliance educating the Heroic Fire.
E0271.body: Atwood quotes unattributed Latin verse: “Ille pius Cheiron justissimus omnes Inter Nubigenas et Magni Doctor Achillis.” [IV.1 ¶32] (our translation: that pious Cheiron, most just among all the Cloud-born, and teacher of great Achilles). She identifies Cheiron as Power and Motive in alliance, educating the Heroic Fire [IV.1 ¶33]; this reading is hers.

E0272.summary: An old name of Egypt (Cham), from the blackness of its soil according to Plutarch; also a name for the art, which the adept calls too narrow.
E0272.body: Reporting Plutarch, the text calls Egypt the art's “mother land, Cham; for so, during a long period, according to Plutarch, was Egypt denominated, or Chemia” [I.1 ¶5], named from the blackness of her soil. Thus Chemia = Egypt = Cham [I.1 ¶5]. Further, “by the word Chemia, says Plutarch, the seeing pupil of the human eye was also designated, and other black matters” [I.1 ¶5]. Others derive both name and art from Cham [I.1 ¶5]. A footnote cites Suidas: “Chimia est auri et argenti confectio” [I.1 n8] (our translation: Chimia is the making of gold and silver). Quoting an adept, the text rejects those “who pin also the narrow name of Chemia on a science ancient and infinite” [I.2 ¶8].

E0273.summary: Atwood's word for the art in its historical record: chemical books burned, the chemists' divine water, Roman knowledge shown by the lamps.
E0273.body: Atwood uses ‘chemical’ and ‘chemists’ of the art itself in her historical survey: books teaching how to make gold and silver were condemned, so that “every chemical book was to be seized and burned together in the public market-place” [I.1 ¶18]; she mentions “a divine water of the chemists” [I.1 ¶20] and Roman knowledge of the art shown by the lamps [I.1 ¶20].

E0274.summary: In the Table Talk, fantastic forms the imaginative spirit makes in the ether when the seeking light enters it; all must be destroyed.
E0274.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes fantastic forms that the imaginative spirit makes in the ether when the seeking light enters it, and says “These Chimaeras have all to be destroyed” [APP ¶171]. The context suggests these are illusory images to be cleared away in the inward work.

E0275.summary: A murky enveloping medium through whose circumference the intellect penetrates to reach the lapsed soul; not further explained.
E0275.body: Atwood speaks of the intellect penetrating “the murky circumference of the chloric ether” [II.3 ¶11] to reach the lapsed soul. The term is not further explained.

E0276.summary: An unnamed chronicle Atwood cites for the lasting visibility in Paris, as late as 1740, of Flamel's charities and symbols of the art.
E0276.body: Atwood cites a chronicle in support of the lasting evidence of Flamel in Paris as late as 1740: “the evidence of his charitable deeds remained and the symbols of the art” [I.1 ¶58].

E0277.summary: A chronicle Atwood cites for its praise of Albert at his death.
E0277.body: Atwood cites the Chronicon Magnum Belgicum for its praise of Albert at his death: “magnus in magia, major in philosophia, maximus in theologia” [I.1 ¶41] (our translation: great in magic, greater in philosophy, greatest in theology).

E0279.summary: Cited from De Nat. Deor. on the ether as an igneous nature begetting all things, and from De Legibus on the Initia as a beginning of a life of reason.
E0279.body: Atwood cites Cicero, De Nat. Deor., lib. ii, in support of the ether as an igneous nature begetting all things: “coelestis alstissima aethereaque natura” [I.2 ¶16] (our translation: the celestial, highest and ethereal nature). She also cites De Legibus, lib. 2, cap. 14, in support of the Initia as the beginning of a life of reason and virtue and of the hope of immortality [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n6]. She uses him with approval.

E0280.summary: The movement of being and, in the work, the rising and falling of the life-principles between heaven and earth by which they are rectified and exalted; the Stone is completed in three.
E0280.body:
Atwood uses circulation in two related senses. Of being as a whole: “And all things in that ultimate circulation are diaphanous” [II.4 ¶50], whereas “But in the sensible world the circulation of things is altogether different” [II.4 ¶50], since there it is broken at the circumference (compare center / circumference). The Vital Spirit ascends and descends in ‘successive circulations’ [II.4 ¶50].

In the practical work, circulation is the upward and downward movement of the life-principles between heaven and earth, which rectifies and exalts them: the operator proceeds “by carrying the circulation upward through a Third principle for reprobation” [IV.2 ¶20]; the matter is “Thus exalted by a rotary circulation” [IV.2 ¶32]; and the Stone is “completed in three successive circulations” [IV.2 ¶33].

E0281.summary: What encloses the hidden Reason; it must undergo resolution before the Reason can awaken.
E0281.body: Atwood says the hidden Reason cannot awaken “without a resolution of the whole circulatory confine” [II.4 ¶39]. The term is not further defined.

E0282.summary: The medium by which the hypostatic unit is multiplied throughout life; not further defined.
E0282.body: Atwood says the hypostatic unit is multiplied “by the circulatory medium throughout life” [IV.2 ¶37]. The term is not further defined.
